standard_name: Cyclic-dominance (cyclic CA / rock-paper-scissors-type) dynamics on a coevolving network with homophilic rewiring; active vs fragmented-frozen phases
citations: Demirel, Prizak, Reddy & Gross, Opinion formation and cyclic dominance in adaptive networks, EPJ B 84, 541 (2011), arXiv:1011.1124
Adaptive cyclically dominating game on co-evolving networks, EPJ B (2017), arXiv:1605.03370
Szolnoki et al., Cyclic dominance in evolutionary games: A review, arXiv:1408.6828
Holme & Newman coevolving voter model (rewire to same-opinion node)
notes: Agree with KNOWN, but the first pass's 'freezes in 1-2 steps' argument conflicts with the persistent late-run oscillation, so the implementation evidently leaves some mismatched links each step. Oscillation is inherited from rule 1 alone (0.82) and is weakened by rewiring, shrinking at larger size and longer runs: consistent with slow approach to the known fragmented absorbing phase. Edge turnover ~0.98 and unchanged with run length, so it probably counts all links ever rewired (mostly the initial burst). Knock-out comparison is weak because both features are zero by definition without interaction. No new phenomenology.
full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** I agree with the first pass's verdict, but not with how it got there. Its main argument, that the system freezes within one or two steps, is contradicted by your evidence.

**Where the first pass goes wrong.** It says that after one rewiring pass every link joins same-type nodes, so nothing can happen afterwards. That doesn't fit your data. Oscillation is still clearly non-zero in the late part of the run (0.27 even at 3x run length), so links between different types must keep reappearing. Most likely the code doesn't rewire every mismatched link in a single sweep, for example because updates are sequential or capped per node. So the reasoning is wrong for the program you actually ran, even if the conclusion is right.

**Why the behaviour is still documented.** What you see is cyclic "type t gives way to t+1" dynamics running alongside homophilic rewiring. Both the active phase and the fragmented frozen phase are described for exactly this kind of model:
- **Demirel, Prizak, Reddy & Gross (2011)** studied cyclic dominance where a link is selected randomly and the game is played between the nodes connected by the link. The loser either adopts the opinion of the winner or rewires the link.
- **The adaptive rock-paper-scissors model (Physica/EPJ B 2017)** reports two phases. An active phase for p < p_c has one connected network of agents using different strategies who are continually interacting and taking adaptive actions. A frozen phase for p > p_c has three separate clusters of agents using only R, P, and S, respectively with terminated adaptive actions.
- **The Szolnoki et al. review of cyclic dominance** concludes that oscillatory behavior in coevolving networks is a robust phenomenon. It also notes that similar results were also reported for a four-strategy cyclic dominance game.
- **Rule 1 on its own** is the textbook cyclic cellular automaton: a cell advances to its next state if any neighbour already carries that successor state.
- **Homophilic rewiring on its own** is the coevolving voter model's rule. he has a probability p to cut the link to the neighbor and rewire it to a randomly chosen agent of the same opinion.

Your 4 types, threshold of 1, every-step updates and lack of probabilities are differences in the rules, not in the behaviour.

**Is it trivial or an artifact?** Partly, judging from your own numbers:
- **Oscillation** is real cyclic-automaton cycling, but it comes almost entirely from rule 1. Rule 1 alone gives 0.82; the full system gives less (0.52). It also shrinks at 4x size (0.36) and at 3x run length (0.27). That looks like a slow drift toward the documented fragmented frozen state, not a new sustained rhythm.
- **Edge turnover** is near saturation (0.98) and doesn't change between the normal and 3x runs. That suggests it counts every link rewired over the whole run, so it mostly reflects the initial rewiring burst rather than ongoing churn. Rule 2 alone already gives 0.74.
- **The knock-out comparison is weak.** Both features are by definition zero without interaction, so passing the "3 spreads from knock-out" test is automatic.

So the coupling adds no new pattern. It just weakens the inherited cycling while the network separates into single-type groups.

**Searches I ran:** coevolving/adaptive rock-paper-scissors with rewiring and oscillations; cyclic cellular automata (excitable dynamics) on adaptive rewiring networks with fragmentation.
